raw_case_text:
A 53-year-old male patient was admitted to a local hospital with recurrent fever and cough in December 2013. He had a smoking history of 40 years, but there was neither immunosuppressive drug intake nor underlying diseases such as tuberculosis, diabetes, and malignancies. Physical examination and laboratory findings were normal except for a body temperature of 37.8 C. Chest computed tomography (CT) showed a 3 x 3 cm mass in the right middle lobe along with multiple nodules in both lungs (fig. 1a). A thoracoscopic wedge resection of the lesion was then performed, and the biopsy showed suppurative granulomatous inflammation. The patient's symptoms improved after surgery and 1 week's use of piperacillin-tazobactam.
However, he was readmitted with cough, fever, and new-onset low back pain in May 2014. Chest CT scan indicated an emerging nodular lesion in the left lower lobe (fig. 1b), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed bony destruction in the L5 vertebral body and L2/3 pedicle (fig. 1c). Biopsies from both tracheoscopy and percutaneous vertebral puncture showed chronic inflammation. Meanwhile, tissue sections of lung specimens were rechecked and the suggestion was suppurative inflammation probably caused by Nocardia. However, no further pathogenic evidence was provided. Although the patient was treated with antituberculosis drugs empirically, he still had persistent back pain and developed bilateral lower extremity weakness, which prompted surgical intervention including drainage, debridement, decompression, and stabilization of the lumbar spine.
Nevertheless, he suffered from a repeated moderate fever after surgery and was then transferred to our hospital. A 2 x 2 cm soft mass was palpable in the right paravertebral area. Muscle strength was 4/5 for both lower extremities. A new MRI showed deterioration of the imaging findings (fig. 1d). Consequently, we performed a second surgery including removal of the original internal fixation, debridement, decompression, and drainage. A few spore or hypha analogues were visualized in tissue sections with Gomori methenamine-silver stain and periodic acid-Schiff stain (fig. 1e). Then, the patient was initially treated with voriconazole (a loading dose of 6 mg/kg of body weight on the 1st day followed by 4 mg/kg, every 12 h intravenously). Two weeks later, he had pain relief and recovered his normal temperature. Resolution of the lumbar lesions was also distinctly observed. Notably, specimens from the third lumbar surgery primarily for spinal stabilization revealed septate fungal hyphae, dichotomously branching at acute angles (fig. 1f). So far, the patient had taken voriconazole for more than 3 months, and no recurrence was detected. However, the muscle strength of both lower extremities did not improve significantly.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old male presented initially with recurrent fever and cough, followed 5 months after right middle lobe wedge resection by recurrent cough, fever, new-onset low back pain, and progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In December 2013, the patient presented to a local hospital with recurrent fever and cough and underwent thoracoscopic wedge resection of a 3 x 3 cm right middle lobe mass plus 1 week of piperacillin-tazobactam. In May 2014, he was readmitted with cough, fever, and new-onset low back pain; despite empirical antituberculosis therapy and initial lumbar spine debridement/fixation for L5 and L2/3 vertebral destruction, he developed bilateral lower-extremity weakness and persistent postoperative fever, prompting transfer to our hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: 40-year smoking history; no history of immunosuppressive medication, tuberculosis, diabetes mellitus, or malignancy.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission (December 2013): temperature 37.8 C with otherwise normal physical examination. Upon transfer after first spinal surgery: recurrent moderate fever, a palpable 2 x 2 cm soft mass in the right paravertebral area, and bilateral lower-extremity motor strength of 4/5.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine baseline laboratory tests on initial admission were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: December 2013 chest CT showed a 3 x 3 cm right middle lobe mass and bilateral pulmonary nodules; thoracoscopic wedge resection histopathology showed suppurative granulomatous inflammation (retrospectively suspected on slide review to be Nocardia without microbiological proof). May 2014 chest CT showed a new left lower lobe nodule, and lumbar MRI revealed bony destruction of the L5 vertebral body and L2/3 pedicle; tracheoscopic and percutaneous vertebral biopsies showed chronic inflammation. Repeat lumbar MRI upon transfer showed worsening spondylodiscitis/paravertebral progression.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated pulmonary and lumbar vertebral aspergillosis (Aspergillus spondylodiscitis and pneumonia, initially misattributed to Nocardia and tuberculosis) was confirmed during second and third lumbar spine surgeries (hardware removal, debridement, decompression, drainage, and restabilization), where tissue sections stained with Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) demonstrated septate fungal hyphae branching dichotomously at acute angles. Treatment with intravenous voriconazole (6 mg/kg loading dose q12h on day 1, then 4 mg/kg q12h) followed by >3 months of voriconazole resolved his fever, back pain, and lumbar lesions without recurrence, though mild bilateral lower-extremity weakness (4/5) persisted.
